title: Room 39 to Goldeneye: the Naval Intelligence Officer Who Invented an Englishman
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Green Street and the Purbeck Coast

stops.name: 27 Green Street, Mayfair, the second son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In a townhouse at 27 Green Street, Mayfair, a second son is born to Valentine Fleming, Conservative member for Henley, and Evelyn Ste Croix Rose. The money is one generation old and enormous; Robert Fleming, the grandfather, came out of Dundee and founded the merchant bank that carries the name. The child is given Lancaster for a middle name and a quarter of London that runs on clubs, tailors, and accounts nobody discusses. Fifty-six years later he is famous for inventing a man who moves through this same square mile and never says where his money comes from.
suggested_refs: The Green Street terraces of Mayfair as they stood before the 1930s rebuilding

stops.name: Braziers Park, Ipsden, the nursery that becomes a library
stops.date_confidence: the family's residence 1906-1911 is attested; no month within it is recorded, so the stop defaults to January
stops.campa: Valentine Fleming buys Braziers Park above Ipsden in 1906 and the family keeps it until 1911, so the whole of Ian's infancy passes in Oxfordshire chalk country rather than in town. The nursery he sleeps in becomes, in a later century, the library of the communal college that occupies the house and still points the room out to visitors. Nothing survives from these years in his own hand. The place enters his record through the deeds and through the family's own telling, and the village of Ipsden retains no memory of the child at all.
suggested_refs: Braziers Park house and its library, the former Fleming nursery

stops.name: Durnford School, Langton Matravers, the father killed
stops.date_confidence: the 1914 start is attested; the term date is conventional
stops.campa: He boards at Durnford, a preparatory school at Langton Matravers on the Purbeck coast, run on cold baths, sea bathing, and long walks over the chalk rather than on scholarship. In May 1917, while he is a pupil here, Valentine Fleming is killed at Gillemont Farm near Epehy on the Western Front. Winston Churchill writes the appreciation The Times prints on the twenty-fifth. The father becomes a photograph on a wall and a standard four sons are measured against; the eldest, Peter, will meet it, and Ian will not.
suggested_refs: Churchill, 'Valentine Fleming. An appreciation,' The Times, 25 May 1917

stops.name: Eton College, the Victor Ludorum and the drift
stops.date_confidence: 1921 entry attested; term date conventional
stops.campa: He enters Eton in his brother Peter's shadow and stays five years in it. On the running track he is unanswerable, holding the Victor Ludorum for two of the years between 1925 and 1927; in the classroom his masters record drift, insolence, and a talent kept just out of use. He leaves a term early to be crammed for the army entrance. Peter takes a first at Oxford and publishes a bestseller before he is thirty. Ian is known instead for his cars and his women, and for a promise nobody expects him to keep. He carries that reputation for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: Eton College athletic records, Victor Ludorum 1925-1927

stops.name: Royal Military College, Sandhurst, the commission not taken
stops.date_confidence: entry 1926 and departure 1927 are attested; the month of entry is not recorded
stops.campa: His mother, who controls the money and therefore the decisions, sends him to the Royal Military College at Sandhurst to be made into an officer. He is there under a year. He contracts gonorrhoea from a woman in London, the matter travels up to the commandant, and Eve Fleming removes him before the course ends rather than let him take a commission into a cavalry regiment being mechanised. The army closes to him at eighteen. The service that will eventually use him is one nobody in the family has thought of.
suggested_refs: Royal Military College Sandhurst cadet registers, 1926-1927

stops.name: The Tennerhof, Kitzbuhel, taught to write
stops.date_confidence: 1927-1928 attested; no month recorded
stops.campa: Eve Fleming sends him to the Tennerhof at Kitzbuhel, a small academy in the Tyrol kept by Ernan Forbes Dennis, lately a British passport control officer in Vienna, and his wife the novelist Phyllis Bottome. The stated object is the Foreign Office examination. What the household actually teaches is Adlerian psychology, skiing, and the pleasures of the continent, and Bottome sets him to writing fiction. He is happier here than at any school he has been sent to. His first spy story is written under her eye and is never published.
suggested_refs: Phyllis Bottome's memoirs of the Tennerhof and her Kitzbuhel pupils

stops.name: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat, Munich, the German
stops.date_confidence: sources give the continental studies as roughly 1927-1931 and place Munich in 1928; no month recorded
stops.campa: He reads at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat in Munich as part of the same continental repair. Weimar Munich is febrile and half-bankrupt, five years from delivering the Reich its capital of the movement, and it leaves him fluent German, an ear for the way Germans talk to each other, and nothing whatever a Foreign Office board will reward. Twelve years later the language is an operational asset in Room 39. In 1928 it is an accomplishment belonging to a young man with no profession and no prospect of one.
suggested_refs: Matriculation records of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat for the 1928 sessions

stops.name: University of Geneva, the examination failed
stops.date_confidence: 1929-1930 given by the biographies; no month recorded
stops.campa: He continues at the University of Geneva, adding French, and courts Monique Panchaud de Bottomes, to whom he is briefly engaged before his mother ends it. He sits the Foreign Office entrance examination and passes to an adequate standard without being offered a post. Sixty-two candidates compete; the biographies place him twenty-fifth, and the version in which he comes seventh and misses by two places is a later improvement on the record. At twenty-two he has four languages, no degree, and no career.
suggested_refs: Foreign Office entrance examination results, 1931 competition

stops.name: Reuters, London, the discipline of the wire
stops.date_confidence: October 1931 attested for the start; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Rejected by the Foreign Office, he goes to Reuters as a sub-editor and journalist, and the wire service does what Eton, Sandhurst, and three universities did not. It teaches him to file: short sentences, checked facts, the deadline ahead of the style. He will demand exactly this of himself in Jamaica twenty years later and describe the method almost in a sub-editor's terms. At Reuters he also learns who pays for information that crosses a border, and what they are paying for.
suggested_refs: Reuters staff records for 1931-1933; the agency's City offices before the Fleet Street move

stops.name: House of the Unions, Moscow, the Metro-Vickers trial
stops.date_confidence: April 1933 attested; the day of his filing is not recorded here
stops.campa: Reuters sends him to Moscow to cover the trial of six British engineers of Metropolitan-Vickers, charged with sabotage and espionage in the Hall of Columns of the House of the Unions. He files the verdict fast enough to beat the field and then, on his own initiative, writes to Stalin asking for an interview. The refusal comes back signed. Fleming keeps that letter for the rest of his life. He has watched a show trial from the press bench at twenty-four, and he has watched it work.
suggested_refs: Reuters archive dispatches from the Metropolitan-Vickers trial, April 1933

stops.name: Rowe and Pitman, Bishopsgate, the indifferent broker
stops.date_confidence: 1935 attested for the move; no month recorded
stops.campa: He leaves journalism in October 1933 for merchant banking at Cull and Co, and in 1935 moves to the stockbrokers Rowe and Pitman on Bishopsgate. By his own account and his colleagues' he is an indifferent banker and a worse broker: competent, unenthusiastic, watching the City rather than working it. What the years buy him is a standing in the world that will matter in 1939. He dines with the men who run things, and he is liked by people who do not otherwise like journalists.
suggested_refs: Partnership records of Cull and Co and Rowe and Pitman, 1933-1939

stops.name: Kitzbuhel, the private country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the biographies place recurring visits through the 1930s and date the meeting with Muriel Wright to this decade without a year
stops.campa: He goes back to Kitzbuhel through the nineteen thirties on skiing holidays, to the same valley the Tennerhof taught him, and there meets Muriel Wright, who becomes his mistress for most of the decade. The Tyrol is his private country, unattached to London offices or to his mother's arrangements, and the one place his biographers find him unguarded. War closes it. He next crosses this continent in uniform, holding a naval rank and the Admiralty designation 17F.
suggested_refs: Kitzbuhel hotel registers of the 1930s British skiing set

stops.name: The Admiralty, Room 39, personal assistant to the Director
stops.date_confidence: recruitment May 1939, commission July 1939, full-time August 1939 all attested; days not recorded
stops.campa: Rear Admiral John Godfrey, Director of Naval Intelligence, recruits him out of stockbroking in May 1939; in July he is commissioned lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, and in August he takes a desk in Room 39 of the Admiralty, overlooking Horse Guards Parade, under the designation 17F. He is Godfrey's personal assistant, which in practice means he sees everything and signs nothing. Within months he is a lieutenant commander, and he holds the desk until the war ends.
suggested_refs: Donald McLachlan, Room 39: Naval Intelligence in Action 1939-45 (1968)

stops.name: The Admiralty, the Trout Memo and item twenty-eight
stops.date_confidence: the memorandum is dated to the day; the authorship is contested, the document being issued over Godfrey's name
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of September a memorandum goes out over Godfrey's name listing schemes for deceiving the enemy, ending at item twenty-eight with a corpse dressed as a courier and dropped in the sea. Men who read it hear the assistant's voice in it; Ben Macintyre attributes it to Fleming outright, and the signature is Godfrey's. Item twenty-eight becomes Operation Mincemeat. Fleming is also credited with proposing that Naval Intelligence use Aleister Crowley, whom Theodor Reuss admitted to the O.T.O. in London and who will write to Dion Fortune from Hastings, to help interrogate Rudolf Hess.
stops.quote: The following suggestion is used in a book by Basil Thomson: a corpse dressed as an airman, with despatches in his pockets, could be dropped on the coast, supposedly from a parachute that has failed. I understand there is no difficulty in obtaining corpses at the Naval Hospital, but, of course, it would have to be a fresh one.
stops.quote_source: Naval Intelligence Division memorandum (the 'Trout Memo'), 29 September 1939, issued over Admiral Godfrey's name
suggested_refs: The Trout Memo, item 28, and its execution as Operation Mincemeat in 1943

stops.name: The Admiralty, Operation Ruthless proposed
stops.date_confidence: the proposal is dated to the day in the printed text
stops.campa: He writes a memorandum to Godfrey proposing that a captured German bomber be crewed by five men in Luftwaffe uniform, one of them word-perfect in German, and ditched in the Channel beside a German rescue boat, which would then be seized with its Enigma machine and its codebooks. The scheme is called Ruthless. The aircraft is found and the crew picked; the rescue boat never appears in the right water, and the operation is cancelled. Alan Turing and Peter Twinn come to Frank Birch at Bletchley about the cancellation like undertakers cheated of a corpse.
stops.quote: I suggest we obtain the loot by the following means: 1. Obtain from Air Ministry an air-worthy German bomber. 2. Pick a tough crew of five, including a pilot, W/T operator and word-perfect German speaker...
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming to Rear Admiral John Godfrey, 12 September 1940, printed in Mavis Batey, 'From Bletchley with Love' (Bletchley Park Trust, 2008), pp. 2-6
suggested_refs: Frank Birch's letter of 20 October 1940 on the cancellation of Ruthless
sources: Mavis Batey, From Bletchley with Love (2008)

stops.name: Tangier International Zone, the fallback office
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month recorded, so the stop defaults to January and is placed before the Iberian tour on that basis alone
stops.campa: Golden Eye, the plan Fleming has been drawing up since August 1940, assumes that Spain may join the Axis and that Gibraltar may be occupied. Tangier, then an international zone thick with the agents of six services, is designated the fallback: a contingency office ready to take over the Rock's signals function the day the Rock stops answering. The scheme is a stay-behind network before the phrase exists, communications and resistance kept alive under an occupation that never comes. It runs to August 1943 and gives its name to a house in Jamaica.
suggested_refs: Operation Golden Eye planning files, Naval Intelligence Division, 1940-1943

stops.name: British Embassy, Madrid, Alan Hillgarth's shadow service
stops.date_confidence: February 1941 attested; no day recorded
stops.campa: In Madrid he works with Alan Hillgarth, naval attache and the man running Britain's shadow operation in Spain: bribery of Franco's generals with American money, charm at the right dinners, bluff where neither will serve. Hillgarth is a novelist before he is an attache, and he shows Fleming what a secret service actually does in a neutral country, which is mostly to pay people and to wait. It is the closest Fleming comes in the whole war to the thing he will later write, and he is a passenger in it.
suggested_refs: Alan Hillgarth's Madrid reports on the subsidy of Spanish generals, 1940-1943

stops.name: The Convent, Gibraltar, the Rock inspected
stops.date_confidence: the visit is dated 16-26 February 1941 in the planning files
stops.campa: He crosses to Gibraltar and works from the Convent, the Governor's residence on Main Street, for ten days, inspecting signals security and setting the Golden Eye machinery in place: the caves, the wireless sets, the men who would be left behind when the garrison went. From the Rock the Strait is nine miles wide and Spanish guns look down into the harbour. He is thirty-two, a lieutenant commander who has never been shot at, standing on the ground where an invasion that never comes would have begun.
suggested_refs: The Convent, Gibraltar, and the Golden Eye stay-behind installations in the Rock's galleries

stops.name: Casino Estoril, the table he cannot document
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates this stopover to May 1941 while dating the Iberian tour to February; the contradiction is left standing and no day is recorded
stops.campa: On an Iberian leg of the same war he stops near Lisbon, where every belligerent's agents drink in the same hotels, and the tradition holds that he gambled one evening at the Casino Estoril against men he took for Germans, lost steadily, and enjoyed outlasting them at the table. Every biographer repeats it. None can source it past Fleming's own retelling. Twelve years later he opens his first novel in a casino at Royale-les-Eaux with a man losing to another man in front of witnesses, on purpose.
suggested_refs: Casino Estoril during the neutral-Portugal years, 1940-1945
sources: John Pearson, The Life of Ian Fleming (1966)

stops.name: British Embassy, Washington, the memorandum for Donovan
stops.date_confidence: the May 1941 trip is attested; the 25 May date is the geography lens figure and is not corroborated to the day elsewhere
stops.campa: He flies to the United States with Godfrey to build Anglo-American intelligence cooperation, and works out of the British Embassy on Massachusetts Avenue. He meets William Donovan, the New York lawyer President Roosevelt is about to make Coordinator of Information, and drafts a long memorandum on how an American secret service ought to be constructed. Donovan's office becomes the OSS and the OSS becomes the CIA. The memorandum's part in that has been enlarged in every retelling since, Fleming's own included.
suggested_refs: Fleming's memorandum to Donovan on the structure of an American intelligence service, 1941

stops.name: Camp X, Whitby, the school he may not have attended
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the visit is claimed rather than documented, the claim is contested by David Stafford's work, and no month is given
stops.campa: Camp X, William Stephenson's British Security Coordination school on the shore of Lake Ontario, teaches sabotage, silent killing, and wireless to agents bound for occupied Europe. Fleming is said to have trained there, or at least to have visited. The school's own chroniclers make the claim; David Stafford's scholarship takes it apart, and the book that carries most of the story, A Man Called Intrepid, is not one that can be relied upon by itself. Stephenson, however, Fleming named in print without any hedge at all.
stops.quote: James Bond is a highly romanticised version of a true spy. The real thing is... William Stephenson.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, foreword to H. Montgomery Hyde, 'Room 3603: The Story of the British Intelligence Center in New York During World War II'
suggested_refs: David Stafford's critique of the Camp X legends; Hyde, Room 3603, with Fleming's foreword
sources: William Stevenson, A Man Called Intrepid (1976)

stops.name: The Admiralty, the pinch unit proposed
stops.date_confidence: March 1942 attested for the proposal; no day recorded
stops.campa: He proposes to Godfrey a unit that will go in with the assault troops and take the things that cannot be bombed: cipher machines, codebooks, charts, the papers in the safe of a naval headquarters before anyone thinks to burn them. It becomes 30 Commando, later 30 Assault Unit, and Fleming runs its targeting from London. In the same year, across the Atlantic, the American Office of Naval Intelligence recruits Meyer Lansky as its go-between on the New York waterfront, under the name Operation Underworld.
stops.quote: to accompany forward troops when a port or naval installation is being attacked and, if the attack is successful, their duty is to capture documents, cyphers
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming's proposal memorandum to Rear Admiral John Godfrey, March 1942
suggested_refs: The founding papers of 30 Commando, Naval Intelligence Division, 1942

stops.name: Off Dieppe, the raid watched from HMS Fernie
stops.date_confidence: the raid is dated to the day; whether 30 Commando was deployed there at all is disputed in the literature
stops.campa: He watches the Dieppe Raid from the destroyer HMS Fernie, offshore, with a party detailed to seize German naval material once the town is taken. The town is not taken. More than half the raiding force is killed, wounded, or captured within hours, and the intelligence party never lands. Fleming had proposed the pinch unit five months earlier, so Dieppe does not originate the idea; it tests the idea and returns nothing. Some accounts make this 30AU's first deployment and other accounts deny the unit was there.
suggested_refs: Nicholas Rankin, Ian Fleming's Commandos (2011), on the Dieppe intelligence party

stops.name: Kingston Harbour, the island decided on
stops.date_confidence: July 1943 per Matthew Parker; the chronology lens gives 1942, and that discrepancy is not resolved here
stops.campa: An Anglo-American naval intelligence conference brings him to Jamaica in July 1943, and between sessions his friend Ivar Bryce drives him along the north coast. Fleming tells him that when the war ends he intends to live on this island and do nothing else. He is thirty-five, running a commando unit by remote control from a room in Whitehall, and he settles the rest of his life in the course of an afternoon's drive. He buys the land three years later, on the coast road east of Ocho Rios.
suggested_refs: Matthew Parker, Goldeneye: Where Bond Was Born (2014), on the 1943 conference
sources: Matthew Parker, Goldeneye: Where Bond Was Born (2014)

stops.name: Naples, the unit in Italy and a Fleming who is not one
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1944 is given without a month for the unit's Naples operations, and Fleming's own visits to Mediterranean commands are undated
stops.campa: 30 Assault Unit works through Naples as the Allied line grinds north, after torpedo research, naval archives, and anything in an Italian or German office worth carrying away. Fleming directs from London and visits Mediterranean commands to see what the unit is producing. In the same city, two decades earlier, Richard Fleming had withdrawn from Lake Maggiore and died in 1922: husband of Antoinette de Saint Leger, no relation whatever, a surname the atlas has to keep from being mistaken for this one.
suggested_refs: 30 Assault Unit target lists for the Italian campaign, 1943-1944

stops.name: London, barred from the field on the day of the landings
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the day of the Normandy landings he is removed as operational head of 30 Assault Unit. The reason is that he knows too much to be allowed near a beach: a man carrying the Ultra secret and the whole target list of Naval Intelligence cannot be permitted to be captured. He stays at his desk in Room 39 while the unit he invented goes ashore. The atlas records his position on the sixth of June as London, since a pin off Normandy would place him precisely where he demonstrably is not.
suggested_refs: The 6 June 1944 change of command in 30 Assault Unit

stops.name: Cherbourg, the paper taken before the fuses
stops.date_confidence: the sources give June to July 1944 for the Cherbourg operations; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: 30 Assault Unit enters Cherbourg behind the fighting to reach the naval headquarters before the demolition parties finish, and comes out with the documents. Fleming, who set the unit's Overlord targets from London, counts the port as proof of the case he put to Godfrey in March 1942: the army takes the ground, and a dozen men behind it take the paper out of the safe. He is not there. He reads what they took in Whitehall, afterwards, at the desk he has not left since 1939.
suggested_refs: 30 Assault Unit reports on the Cherbourg naval headquarters, June 1944

stops.name: Kandy, South East Asia Command
stops.date_confidence: December 1944 to January 1945 attested; no day recorded
stops.campa: He flies to South East Asia Command headquarters at Kandy, in the Ceylon hills, on a fact-finding trip into intelligence liaison in a theatre where the war has a year still to run. It is his one extended sight of Asia in uniform, and he makes it as a staff officer with a notebook rather than as anything else. Twenty years later he sends his agent to a Japanese island to die and be resurrected there, and the far side of the world he uses for it he first crosses now.
suggested_refs: SEAC headquarters at Kandy under Mountbatten, 1944-1945

stops.name: Schloss Tambach, the German naval archive taken whole
stops.date_confidence: the seizure is dated to 11 April 1945; the geography lens gave only the bare year
stops.campa: Western Allied troops reach Schloss Tambach near Coburg on the eleventh of April and find inside it the archive of the German navy, moved there in 1943 for safekeeping, together with part of the records of the Reich Air Ministry. 30 Assault Unit takes it. The German navy itself is not old, dating from 1848 and 1871, but the Prussian material bound into the archive runs back further, and the haul is the largest single capture the unit makes. Fleming counts it the vindication of an idea he had at a desk in 1942.
suggested_refs: The Marinearchiv at Schloss Tambach, seized 11 April 1945

stops.name: London, demobilised into the Kemsley papers
stops.date_confidence: May 1945 attested for both the demobilisation and the Kemsley appointment; no day recorded
stops.campa: He is demobilised in May and takes, in the same month, the post of foreign manager of the Kemsley newspaper group, which owns the Sunday Times: a network of correspondents in the world's capitals, answering to him. The contract allows him two months' leave every winter, and he takes it in writing before he takes the job. He has negotiated, at thirty-seven, the exact conditions of the next nineteen years: an apparatus to run from London, and January and February in Jamaica to do with as he likes.
suggested_refs: Fleming's Kemsley contract and the Mercury foreign service, 1945-1959

stops.name: Goldeneye, Oracabessa, the house on the cliff
stops.date_confidence: the 1946 purchase of fifteen acres is attested; the chronology lens gives 1945 for the building, and no month is recorded either way
stops.campa: He buys fifteen acres next to the Golden Clouds estate at Oracabessa and builds on the cliff above a private cove a flat concrete house with no glass in the windows, three bedrooms, and a jalousied main room open to the weather. He calls it Goldeneye, after the Iberian operation and, by another account, after a Carson McCullers novel. The desk faces away from the sea so the view cannot get at him. For the next eighteen winters this house is where he is, and the rest of the year is where he waits.
suggested_refs: Matthew Parker, Goldeneye: Where Bond Was Born (2014)
sources: Matthew Parker, Goldeneye: Where Bond Was Born (2014)

stops.name: Goldeneye, Casino Royale written in five weeks
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the writing runs 15 January to 16 February 1952
stops.campa: He begins writing on the fifteenth of January and finishes on the sixteenth of February: two thousand words a day, three hours in the morning and an hour before dinner, nothing reread and nothing corrected until the whole thing is done. He is forty-three, about to be married for the first time, and has told friends for years that he will one day write the spy story to end all spy stories. Casino Royale opens at a card table at three in the morning with a man who has been playing too long.
stops.quote: I write for about three hours in the morning ... and I do another hour's work between six and seven in the evening. I never correct anything and I never go back to see what I have written ... By following my formula, you write 2,000 words a day.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, article on his method, Books and Bookmen, May 1963, describing the Goldeneye routine
suggested_refs: The writing desk at Goldeneye, turned away from the sea
sources: Faulks and Fleming, Devil May Care (2009), p. 320

stops.name: Jamaica, the marriage to Ann Charteris
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pin is Goldeneye, the sources naming only Jamaica
stops.campa: He marries Ann Charteris in Jamaica on the twenty-fourth of March, thirteen years after the affair began, she having been married first to the third Baron O'Neill and then to Viscount Rothermere, who divorced her naming Fleming. A stillborn daughter, Mary, had been born to them in 1948 while she was still Rothermere's wife. Their son Caspar is born in London in August. The book written at the desk in the next room two months before the wedding is the reason the marriage is remembered at all.
suggested_refs: The Rothermere divorce proceedings of 1951, in which Fleming was named

stops.name: London, Casino Royale published
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Jonathan Cape publishes Casino Royale on the thirteenth of April in a first printing of four thousand seven hundred and twenty-eight copies, under a cover Fleming designed himself. It sells out inside a month and goes to three printings. The hero carries the name of the American ornithologist whose Birds of the West Indies sits on the shelf at Goldeneye, borrowed because Fleming wanted the flattest name available to him. The American paperback of 1955 renames the book You Asked for It and the hero Jimmy Bond.
stops.quote: By God, [James Bond] is the dullest name I ever heard.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, interview, The New Yorker, 1962
suggested_refs: The Jonathan Cape first edition of Casino Royale, cover design by Fleming

stops.name: Saratoga Race Course, the American reportage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1954 is given for the Diamonds Are Forever research trip without a month, and the Saratoga meeting runs in August
stops.campa: Researching Diamonds Are Forever he goes to the Saratoga track and the touts and fixers and mud-bath establishments around it, then west across the continent to Las Vegas, still a raw casino town on a desert road rather than the spectacle it becomes. He works the way a foreign manager works: he goes, he looks, he writes it down, and the notes go into the novel without much softening. The American middle of that book is reportage with a plot laid over it.
suggested_refs: Fleming's 1954 American notebooks for Diamonds Are Forever

stops.name: Pera, Istanbul, the man who becomes Darko Kerim
stops.date_confidence: June 1955 attested for the Interpol conference; no day recorded
stops.campa: The Sunday Times sends him to Istanbul to cover an Interpol conference, and he stays in the old European quarter above the Golden Horn. His fixer is Nazim Kalkavan, a Turkish shipping man educated at Oxford, who talks for days while Fleming writes it down in a notebook. Kalkavan goes into From Russia with Love almost untouched as Darko Kerim, head of Station T, and the transcription is close enough that Fleming later admitted it. He does the same with Richard Hughes in Tokyo seven years later.
suggested_refs: Fleming's Istanbul notebook of June 1955, recording Nazim Kalkavan

stops.name: Sirkeci Terminal, out on the Orient Express
stops.date_confidence: the departure falls within the June 1955 visit; no day is recorded in the sources reached
stops.campa: He leaves Istanbul from Sirkeci, the terminus where the line from Paris ends against the Bosphorus, and travels the route his agent will later fight along. He takes down the timetable, the carriage layout, the border stops, and the exact business of a wagon-lit at night, and puts them into the novel as they are. The journey itself is uneventful. The transposition needs nothing invented except the men in the next compartment, and those he supplies out of SMERSH.
stops.quote: Those whom the Gods wish to destroy, they first make bored.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, 'From Russia, with Love' (Jonathan Cape, 1957), Ch. 11
suggested_refs: Sirkeci Terminal and the Simplon Orient Express timetables of 1955

stops.name: Ginza, Tokyo, twelve days for one book
stops.date_confidence: two visits are attested, of three days in 1959 and twelve days in 1962; neither is dated to a month in the sources reached
stops.campa: He comes to Tokyo first for three days on a round-the-world circuit for the Sunday Times, the series collected as Thrilling Cities, and returns in 1962 for twelve days with the Australian correspondent Richard Hughes and the Japanese journalist Torao Saito to do it properly: the baths, the Ginza, the wrestlers, the coastal villages of the ama divers. Everything from the second trip goes into You Only Live Twice, and Hughes and Saito go in as well, as Dikko Henderson and Tiger Tanaka.
suggested_refs: Ian Fleming, Thrilling Cities (1963), the Tokyo chapter

stops.name: London, Kennedy's list and the first heart attack
stops.date_confidence: the Life list is dated 17 March 1961 and the heart attack to April 1961; no day is recorded for the attack
stops.campa: In March, Life magazine prints President Kennedy's list of favourite books and From Russia with Love is on it. American sales, indifferent for eight years, go vertical. Dr. No, which the critics savaged in 1958, is suddenly being read by everyone. In April, at an editorial conference at the Sunday Times, Fleming has a heart attack. He is fifty-two. The success he has wanted since the Reuters newsroom arrives in the same season as the first notice served on him by his own heart, and he has three years to run.
suggested_refs: Life magazine, 17 March 1961, the Kennedy reading list

stops.name: London, the blunt instrument explained
stops.date_confidence: the interview is dated to 1962; no month is recorded in the sources reached
stops.campa: Asked what he thought he was making, he gives the answer that has confounded everyone who came to Bond by any route other than the books. Not a hero: an instrument. The character was to be dull, uninteresting, a man to whom things happen, and the interest was to lie in the things and the places and the equipment rather than in the man holding them. By 1962 the character has escaped him into a readership, a newspaper strip, and an industry. Fleming keeps giving the same answer, and the answer keeps not being wanted.
stops.quote: When I wrote the first one in 1953, I wanted Bond to be an extremely dull, uninteresting man to whom things happened; I wanted him to be a blunt instrument.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, interview, The New Yorker, 1962
suggested_refs: The New Yorker profile of Fleming, 1962

stops.name: Goldeneye, the last January
stops.date_confidence: January 1964 attested for the final Jamaican stay; no day recorded
stops.campa: He comes to Goldeneye in January for the last time and writes the first draft of The Man with the Golden Gun in the usual weeks, at the usual rate, facing away from the usual sea. The draft is thin and he knows it is thin. Since the attack of 1961 the winters have been convalescence with a typewriter set down in the middle of them. He leaves this manuscript without the full editing pass he has given every book since 1952, and it is the last work of his own that he handles at all.
stops.quote: Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
stops.quote_source: Ian Fleming, 'Casino Royale' (Jonathan Cape, 1953), Ch. 20 (Rene Mathis to Bond)

stops.name: Royal St George's, Sandwich, the captain at lunch
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August he drives from his hotel in Canterbury to Royal St George's at Sandwich, the links he has played for years and put into Goldfinger as Royal St Marks, where the match against Auric Goldfinger is fought hole by hole across this ground. He has been elected Captain of the club that year by his predecessor Eric Pemberton. He lunches in the clubhouse. Shortly after the meal he collapses with a heart attack. He is fifty-six, and has held the captaincy a matter of months.
suggested_refs: Royal St George's captaincy records, 1964; the Goldfinger match as 'Royal St Marks'

stops.name: Kent and Canterbury Hospital, on his son's birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The ambulance takes him twenty kilometres west to the Kent and Canterbury Hospital. He apologises to the crew for the trouble and remarks on the speed they make through the traffic, and these are the last words of his that anyone writes down. He dies in the early morning of the twelfth of August, aged fifty-six, on his son Caspar's twelfth birthday. The twelfth Bond novel lies unpolished in a drawer in London, and Jonathan Cape will publish it on the first of April the following year.
stops.quote: I am sorry to trouble you chaps. I don't know how you get along so fast with the traffic on the roads these days.
stops.quote_source: Fleming's last recorded words to the ambulance crew, 12 August 1964, in Andrew Lycett, Ian Fleming (1996), p. 443
suggested_refs: Kent and Canterbury Hospital, Ethelbert Road, Canterbury

stops.name: St James's Church, Sevenhampton, the family plot
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Sevenhampton is attested; no source reached gives the date of the funeral, so the stop is pinned to the day of death
stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard of St James's at Sevenhampton, near Highworth in Wiltshire, beside the house he and Ann had bought, under an obelisk. What is cut on that obelisk no source reached for this journey records. Caspar, who turned twelve the day his father died, dies of a barbiturate overdose in October 1975, aged twenty-three, and goes into the same ground. Ann joins them in 1981. The plot closes over the whole family within seventeen years of the first burial.
suggested_refs: The Fleming obelisk in St James's churchyard, Sevenhampton, Wiltshire

stops.name: Goldeneye, sold to Marley and then to Blackwell
stops.date_confidence: Marley's purchase is dated 1976 and the sale to Blackwell to the following year; no month is recorded
stops.campa: Twelve years after Fleming's death Bob Marley buys the house at Oracabessa, and sells it the year after to Chris Blackwell of Island Records, whose mother Blanche had been Fleming's companion through the Jamaican years. Blackwell turns the estate into the flagship of a hotel group and keeps the desk. Fourteen Bond books were written in this room between 1952 and 1964. Nine writers since have been licensed by the family company to go on writing them, and have done so for more than half a century.
